description: We are a team of software and artificial intelligence developers who have found our ideal environment for growth in hackathons and tech competitions. We combine expertise in web and mobile development, backend systems, and AI model integration, enabling us to take an idea from concept to functional prototype in record time.
summary:
We are Payload: a co-op 3D browser game where you design a space mission, fly it with your team and understand why it succeeded or failed.
Designing a real mission means balancing mass, power, budget and schedule. Today there are only very technical simulators, or games that explain nothing.
In Payload you build the ship in a hangar, and a Go/No-Go review tells you what is wrong. Then you fly it, fix failures and send your data to Earth; a final report explains the causes. What sets us apart is sanity: the crew wears down with isolation and distance, works more slowly and makes mistakes, and bringing them back costs time, power and credits.
We use 19 real bodies from NASA and JPL fact sheets, plus NASA’s human risks. Near Jupiter, solar panels deliver 27 times less power: panels or an RTG?
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Payload is a co-op 3D game that runs in the browser for 1 to 4 players. You design a space mission, fly it in real time, and at the end you find out why it succeeded or failed. It follows NASA's mission life cycle in three steps:

1. Design. In the hangar you choose a science objective, instruments, ship modules and a launcher. You have to stay within mass, power, budget and schedule. A Go/No-Go review tells you what is wrong before you can launch.

2. Fly. You fly the ship you designed across a map of 19 real Solar System bodies. You walk inside the ship in first or third person. You fix failures as they happen, manage power, fuel, oxygen and hull, land on surfaces with a jetpack, and collect samples. You also have to wait for contact windows to send your science data back to Earth.

3. Understand. A post-mission report shows the chain of causes behind the result. For example: "the antenna was too weak, so the data never reached Earth."

Each crew member also has sanity, which wears down according to NASA's RIDGE hazards (radiation, isolation, distance, gravity, hostile environment). A stressed crew member works slower and makes small mistakes, but never dies from it. Recovering them costs things that are already scarce: rest time, calls home, provisions, or a habitat module that adds mass and draws power. A guided first mission, "Your first CubeSat," teaches the whole cycle step by step.

Benefits

- It shows the trade-offs of mission design through play, without text-heavy tutorials. If your instrument draws too much power, you feel it in flight.

- It explains the why behind success or failure, which most space games never do.

- Teamwork is built into the game, with crew roles and a shared Go/No-Go vote, the way a real mission team works.

- It's free in a browser, bilingual (Spanish and English), and needs no installation.

Intended impact

We want people who are curious about space, students and teachers to understand how a real mission is designed: why engineers choose solar panels or an RTG, why mass limits your destination, and why the human factor is an engineering decision too. Next we want to measure how much players actually learn and add discipline-based roles, modeled on NASA Goddard's Mission Design Lab.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

- Language: TypeScript (strict mode), in a pnpm monorepo.

- Client: React 19, React Three Fiber, Three.js, Drei, Rapier (physics), Zustand, i18next, Tailwind CSS and Vite.

- Game engine: a pure TypeScript simulation that is deterministic (seeded random numbers, fixed time step). The same code runs in the browser for solo play and on the server for co-op. It's covered by 650+ automated tests (Vitest).

- Multiplayer: an authoritative Colyseus server with room codes and reconnection.

- Content as data: ships, failures, instruments, launchers, missions and Solar System bodies live in JSON catalogs, checked with zod.

- Data sources: NASA Planetary Fact Sheets, the JPL Small-Body Database, the Dawn, OSIRIS-REx and Psyche (NASA) and Hayabusa2 (JAXA) missions, NASA's Human Research Program risks, CubeSat 101 and the NASA webinar "Design and Develop Science Missions."

- Deployment: AWS Amplify , AWS EC2 and AWS S3

- Hardware: standard laptops and desktops. We tuned performance on integrated GPUs so it runs on modest school computers.

- AI assistance: Claude Code, with specialized agents for the engine, the 3D client, content, documentation and validation.

How is it creative?

Most mission simulators are technical, and most space games are fun but don't explain anything. Payload connects both: the mission you design becomes the ship you then live inside and keep alive. Crew sanity is our biggest difference. We turned NASA's human-health risks into a resource you manage, and it competes with power, mass and credits. Real physics also drives choices. Solar power drops with the square of the distance to the Sun, about 27 times less at Jupiter than near the Moon. That forces a real decision between solar panels and an RTG.

What factors did the team consider?

- Learning versus fun: distances are compressed and the physics is game physics. It's a learning model, not an orbital simulator, and we say so in the game.

- Accuracy: we use only public data with cited sources. The six fictional map points (stations, transit orbits) are marked as fictional in the game's data files. NASA gives no numbers for sanity effects, so ours are our own design choices.

- Accessibility: bilingual from day one, runs in a browser, works on modest hardware, and explanations are always optional and one line long.

- Co-op and fairness: an authoritative server, the same engine for solo and multiplayer, and deterministic simulation.

- Licensing: every 3D model and asset has its author, source and license recorded. We don't use NASA mascots or marks without authorization.

- Honest limits: keyboard and mouse only for now, and we still need to test with more players and measure
